title: A Baboon's Silvery Fur May Explain Its Link to a Moon God
summary:
One monkey's moonlike color might explain its link to an ancient Egyptian god. In ancient Egypt, Thoth was the god of wisdom, magic and the moon. He took two animal forms: a black-and-white bird called the African sacred ibis, and the silvery hamadryas baboon. But why ancient Egyptians chose these species, especially the baboon, has been a bit of a mystery. A new study now shows that the color of hamadryas baboon fur closely matches that of the moon. The resemblance could explain why these monkeys were chosen to embody a lunar god, the researchers say. They shared their findings in the journal Time and Mind on July 14.

The puzzle caught the attention of Nathaniel Dominy, a primatologist at Dartmouth College. He got curious about the "baboonification" of Thoth while studying primates in Africa. Baboons are not well liked in many parts of Africa, he notes: they feast on farmers' crops and sometimes destroy them without even eating them. Even stranger, baboons are not native to Egypt. Ancient Egyptians imported them as exotic pets. Many gods had animal forms, such as hippos, crocodiles and falcons, Dominy says, but all of those animals lived in ancient Egypt, except the baboon.

So what made the hamadryas baboon so special? A clue came when Egyptologist Julien Cooper traced Thoth's name to an Egyptian root that meant "bright" and "white", words describing moonlight. That hinted the ibis might have been picked for its bright white feathers. Dominy and fellow primatologist Cat Hobaiter, of the University of St Andrews in Scotland, set out to see if color might likewise link baboons to Thoth.

To compare colors objectively, the team used a tool called a spectrometer, which measures how much light of different wavelengths reflects off an object. Dominy took one to the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, where he measured light bouncing off hairs from a dozen olive and hamadryas baboon specimens. The hamadryas profile looked just like moonlight. "I almost cried a little bit! It was just so perfect," Dominy says. The hamadryas fur was also about 65 percent brighter than olive baboon fur, and the silver-white hairs on male hamadryas baboons' cheeks and chests were brighter than those of any other monkey the Egyptians might have known. That boosts the researchers' suspicion that hamadryas baboons embodied Thoth because they reminded ancient Egyptians of moonlight.
why_it_matters: It shows how science can test ideas about the ancient world, and how a simple thing like color may have shaped what people believed thousands of years ago.

background_read: In ancient Egypt, many gods were shown in animal form, and each animal was thought to show something about the god.
Thoth was the god of wisdom, magic, and the moon, and his two animal forms were the ibis and the hamadryas baboon.
Scientists study these links by looking for clues in old writings and by testing things in the real world, such as comparing the color of fur with the color of moonlight.
Color mattered in ancient Egypt because bright white could stand for the moon, so a silvery animal could seem like a natural picture of a moon god.
